category_description: Minimum pay, statutory sick and family pay, student loan repayments and Child Benefit.
subcategory_description: The legal minimum rates of pay, and statutory pay during sickness and family leave.
subject_name: National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage
subject_intro: The legal minimum hourly pay by age and for apprentices, from 1 April 2026.
subject_meta_title: Minimum Wage Rates 2026: National Living Wage £12.71
subject_meta_description: UK minimum wage from April 2026: £12.71 an hour at 21 and over, £10.85 at 18 to 20, and £8 for under-18s and apprentices.
label: National Living Wage (21 and over)
Minimum wage, under 18
context: Per hour, for workers above school leaving age.

label: Apprentice rate
context: Per hour, for apprentices under 19, or 19 and over in the first year of their apprenticeship. Other apprentices get the rate for their age.

subject_intro: The minimum employers must pay staff who are off sick. Since April 2026 it is paid from the first day of sickness, with no minimum earnings test.
subject_meta_title: Statutory Sick Pay 2026/27: Rate and New Rules
subject_meta_description: Statutory Sick Pay for 2026/27 is £123.25 a week or 80% of average weekly earnings if lower, paid from day one of sickness for up to 28 weeks.
label: Statutory Sick Pay (weekly maximum)
context: Employees get this or 80% of their average weekly earnings, whichever is lower. Paid from the first day of sickness since 6 April 2026, when the three unpaid waiting days and the minimum earnings test were abolished.

label: Rate for lower earners
context: Of average weekly earnings, if that comes to less than the weekly maximum.

subject_intro: The minimum pay for employees on maternity or paternity leave in 2026/27, and how long it lasts.
subject_meta_description: Statutory Maternity Pay is 90% of earnings for 6 weeks, then £194.32 a week or 90% if lower for 33 weeks. Paternity Pay is £194.32 or 90% if lower.
label: Maternity Pay, first 6 weeks
context: Of average weekly earnings before tax, with no upper limit.

label: Maternity Pay, weeks 7 to 39 (weekly)
context: Or 90% of average weekly earnings if that is lower.

label: Paternity Pay (weekly)
context: Or 90% of average weekly earnings if that is lower, for one or two weeks.
Employees usually need average earnings of at least this much a week to qualify for Statutory Maternity and Paternity Pay.

subcategory_description: When student loan repayments start and how much is taken from pay.
subject_intro: Student loan repayments start once income passes the threshold for your plan. These are the thresholds and repayment rates for 2026/27.
subject_meta_description: Student loan thresholds for 2026/27: Plan 1 £26,900, Plan 2 £29,385, Plan 4 £33,795, Plan 5 £25,000 and Postgraduate £21,000.
label: Plan 1 threshold (yearly)
context: Older loans, including English and Welsh courses started before September 2012 and Northern Ireland loans.

label: Plan 2 threshold (yearly)
context: English and Welsh courses started between September 2012 and July 2023. The government has said this threshold will be frozen from April 2027.

label: Plan 5 threshold (yearly)
context: English courses started from August 2023. Repayments began in April 2026.

label: Repayment rate (Postgraduate)
context: Of income above the threshold, and paid on top of any undergraduate repayments.

subcategory_description: Payments and tax rules for families with children.
subject_name: Child Benefit Rates and the High Income Charge
subject_intro: How much Child Benefit pays each week in 2026/27, and when higher earners start paying it back through the High Income Child Benefit Charge.
subject_meta_title: Child Benefit 2026/27: Weekly Rates and High Income Charge
subject_meta_description: Child Benefit for 2026/27 is £27.05 a week for the eldest child and £17.90 for each other child, clawed back from incomes between £60,000 and £80,000.
label: Eldest or only child (weekly)
context: There is no limit on the number of children you can claim for.

label: High Income Child Benefit Charge starts above
context: Based on the adjusted net income of the higher earner in the household. The charge is 1% of the benefit for every £200 of income above this.

label: Child Benefit fully repaid at
context: It can still be worth claiming, since the claim gives the carer National Insurance credits towards the State Pension.
